purpose: Hold draft language patterns for lay and practitioner surfaces without treating them as final scripts.

phrases.usable_shape: You can speak in an ordinary voice if that feels right. Silence is also allowed.
At this stage, comfort may mean mouth care and not pressuring food or drink. Ask the care team what is safe.
That sound can be frightening to hear. The care team can help you check comfort and whether anything should be changed.
avoid: This means they have exactly hours left.

phrases.usable_shape: You do not have to argue with what they are seeing. Keep them safe, speak simply, and call the care team if you are worried.
Use the care plan and local contact number. In some expected home deaths, there may be room to pause, but the required steps depend on where you are.
It is okay not to know what to do with the medicines or equipment. Leave them as they are until the relevant team tells you.

phrases.scene: wanting to go home or leave
phrases.usable_shape: You can ask gently what home means right now. Do not argue, and ask the care team for help if they seem distressed or unsafe.
avoid: You are already home; stop saying that.

phrases.usable_shape: Follow their lead, answer simply within what you know, and involve the care team if they want more information.

phrases.scene: fear, anger, or not wanting to die
phrases.usable_shape: That sounds frightening. I am here with you. We can ask for help with what feels worst right now.
Love, thanks, apology, forgiveness, or goodbye can be offered if they fit; silence and ordinary words can also be enough.
avoid: Say this or you will regret it forever.

phrases.usable_shape: A death can be meaningful without a final sentence. Quiet, ordinary talk, or no response are part of what happens too.
avoid: They would have spoken if they loved you.

phrases.usable_shape: Use words that the person can understand. When clarity matters, simple words like died or dying may help; when quoting family language, preserve their words with context.
You can ask what will happen next before the body is moved. It is also okay to need a moment, as long as local and care-team requirements are followed.
avoid: Do not let them take the body.

phrases.usable_shape: These words are confusing because they mean different things in different systems. Ask the local office or care team which document is meant.
avoid: Just get the death certificate online.
This paperwork is the same everywhere.

phrases.usable_shape: It is reasonable to ask what is required, what is optional, and what each item costs. Local law and provider rules matter.
avoid: A real funeral has to include this.
The cheapest option means you loved them less.

phrases.usable_shape: A wave of grief does not mean you have gone backward. It means something has touched the loss again.
avoid: This proves you are not coping.

phrases.usable_shape: Children usually need clear, concrete information and real choices, not surprises or forced bravery.
avoid: They are too young to grieve.
Make them go so they learn.
